messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Thorne, a 42-year-old ship captain, has always defined himself by his steady hand and unwavering command. That sense of self was fractured nine months ago, during what should have been a routine cargo loading in a South Asian port. A mislabeled container of industrial chemicals, positioned two levels below the bridge, detonated without warning. The initial bang was a deafening, gut-punching force that threw him against the bulkhead. For a moment, the world was a blizzard of white noise and flying metal; he remembers a crewman’s thermos cartwheeling past his head just before a secondary explosion ripped through the deck. In the ensuing chaos, local port authorities and military personnel swarmed the vessel. To Marcus, their crisp uniforms were not a sign of order but of intrusive, unhelpful authority, their shouted commands in a language he didn't understand only adding to the pandemonium. He felt utterly alone, certain that he was the only one who could save his crew, yet powerless to do so. He has come to believe he can’t rely on other people in a crisis.

Since returning home, Marcus’s world has shrunk. The open sea, once a source of solace, now feels menacing and unpredictable. Back on a new vessel, he finds himself constantly scanning the faces of his crew, not for camaraderie, but for signs of threat. He has become vigilant for anyone who seems out of place or dangerous. This has led him to give up important responsibilities he once prided himself on. He no longer performs the final pre-departure walk-through himself, delegating the critical safety check to his first mate. He tells himself it’s about efficiency, but he knows it’s because he can’t bear to be in the confined, noisy cargo hold, a place ripe with potential triggers. At home, his wife, Elena, has noticed the changes. A car backfiring down the street causes Marcus to drop to a crouch. When their neighbor’s son was carelessly throwing a baseball against their shared fence, Marcus stormed out, his reaction so severe it frightened the child. He now refuses to go to new restaurants or social gatherings, stating he can’t go to unfamiliar places because he cannot properly assess the danger. When they do go to their usual diner, he insists on a booth in the corner, his back to the wall, where he can see the door and all the patrons—always choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected he feels.

Sleep offers little respite. Marcus lies awake for hours, his body rigid, convinced he needs to stay alert for any potential threat to his home. He listens to the house settle, interpreting every creak as a potential intruder. To quiet the racing thoughts, he has found a dangerous and temporary solace in online gambling. The sharp thrill of a poker hand, the quick win or loss, is a powerful distraction that cuts through the constant, low-grade anxiety. He actively avoids speaking or even thinking about the explosion, holding the firm belief that if he truly lets the memory in, he will not be able to handle it; the images of the chaos and his own helplessness would simply break him. This internal battle is fueled by a simmering anger. The official report cited corporate negligence but assigned no individual blame. The knowledge that the people responsible have faced no consequences eats at him, a constant, bitter reminder of the injustice. It was after receiving a formal warning from his shipping company, prompted by his first mate’s concerns over his erratic behavior and delegation of core duties, that Marcus finally sought help. He sat in the therapist’s office, a man who had mastered oceans but was now adrift in his own mind, terrified he would lose the one thing that defined him: his command.
